opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting thing is that we're moving from a world where these models are tools you consult to a world where they're genuinely collaborators. For a long time, the way scientists used AI was a bit like using a very good search engine or a calculator: you ask a question, you get an answer, and then you do all the real work yourself. What's changing now, with ChatGPT and especially with Codex, is that the model can actually take on a chunk of the work end to end.

Take Codex, for example. A huge part of modern science is computational. You have an idea, and then you spend days or weeks writing code to run the simulation, clean the data, set up the experiment, debug the pipeline. That's a real bottleneck, and it's not the part where the scientist's unique insight lives. If Codex can take that and turn it from weeks into hours, the scientist can test ten ideas instead of one. That changes the rhythm of discovery.

On the ChatGPT side, what I've been personally amazed by is the reasoning, especially in mathematics. I've seen these models help with real research-level problems: suggesting a lemma, finding a connection to a paper from a field you've never read, or catching a gap in a proof. It's not that the model replaces the mathematician. It's that it widens the surface area of what one person can explore. Science has become so specialized that no one can know everything, and the model is a kind of bridge across all those silos.

So the way I'd put it is: these tools compress the distance between having an idea and knowing whether that idea is any good. And when you compress that loop, you don't just do the same science faster. You start doing different science, more ambitious science, because the cost of trying something bold has gone way down. I think we're at the very beginning of that, and the next few years are going to be quite remarkable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, there are really two stories here, and they're starting to merge.

The first is the one people already know: ChatGPT as a thinking partner. A scientist can come to it with a half-formed idea, a result they don't understand, a paper in a field adjacent to their own, and get something back that's actually useful. That already changed a lot. If you're a mathematician and you want to check a lemma, or you're a biologist and you need to understand a statistical method, you no longer have to wait a week to find the right colleague. And with the reasoning models, I've personally seen it work through problems that I would have given to a strong graduate student. Not always correctly, but often enough that it changes how you spend your day.

The second story is Codex, and I think this is the one that's underappreciated. Most science today is bottlenecked on code. Not on ideas. The idea takes an afternoon, and then you spend three weeks writing the simulation, cleaning the data, fixing the pipeline, getting the plots to work. Codex collapses that. You describe the experiment, it writes the code, runs it, looks at the output, and iterates. So the loop between "I wonder if" and "here's the plot" goes from weeks to hours. That's not a small efficiency gain. That's a different way of doing research, because suddenly you can afford to test ten ideas instead of one.

And where it gets really interesting is when those two come together. You have a system that can reason about the science and also execute. It can say, this hypothesis seems plausible, let me write the code to check it, oh, the data contradicts it, let me revise. That's the scientific method, running at machine speed. We're not fully there yet, I want to be honest about that. These systems still make mistakes, they can be confidently wrong, and the scientist still needs to be in the loop verifying things. But the trajectory is clear.

What I find most exciting is actually not the big flashy breakthroughs. It's the democratization. A small lab without a dozen postdocs can now do work that used to require a big institution. A researcher in a country without a strong computational tradition can run sophisticated analyses. That's going to produce a lot more science, from a lot more places, and I think that's where we'll see the real impact over the next few years.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that scientists can spend more time on the ideas and less time on the friction of turning those ideas into experiments. You have a hypothesis, but testing it might require writing code, learning an unfamiliar tool, or working through a calculation. Codex and ChatGPT can help with those steps, so you can explore more possibilities and get feedback faster.

And then there’s the possibility of using them as thinking partners: asking for another approach, looking for a counterexample, or identifying an assumption you haven’t justified. You still have to check the reasoning and run the experiment. But if that interaction helps you ask a better question, or test an idea you otherwise would have set aside, it can expand what you’re able to do as a scientist.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that every scientist can have a collaborator that helps them move from an idea to an experiment much faster. With Codex, you can describe a simulation or an analysis you want to run, and get help building it. With ChatGPT, you can explore a question, challenge an assumption, or work through an argument.

And those things reinforce each other. You have a hypothesis, you write some code to test it, the result surprises you, and you refine the hypothesis. If AI makes that loop faster, scientists can explore more ideas—including ideas they might otherwise set aside because testing them would take too much effort.

The scientist still has to ask good questions and decide what constitutes convincing evidence. But more of their time can go toward those decisions. That’s the opportunity I find most exciting: expanding what an individual scientist can actually try.
